mostly Easy
tm.ask: the amount in the other unit
tm.rl: Write the factor as a fraction that cancels the unit you have.
hd: Put the unit you have on the bottom of the factor: 77 rods × (5.5 yards / 1 rod).
Smaller unit (more of them): multiply; bigger unit: divide.
tr: Dividing when you should multiply
Answering the unconverted total

tm.nm: Chain two conversion factors
tl: two factors given (8 fluid ounces = 1 cup and 4 cups = 1 quart)
or a density used as a factor (ounces per cubic inch × dollars per ounce)
tm.ask: the amount in the final unit
tm.rl: Line up the fractions so every middle unit cancels.
hd: Write each factor as a fraction; the middle unit must appear once on top and once on the bottom.
Multiply across.
tr: Using only one of the two factors
Dividing by the density instead of multiplying

tm.nm: Convert a rate’s units
tl: a rate (per minute, per hour, km per hour)
“at what rate, in posters per hour”
sometimes the time factor (3,600) is not given
tm.ask: the rate in new units
tm.rl: Convert top and bottom separately; a unit in the denominator flips direction.
hd: Per minute to per hour: × 60 (60 minutes in each hour).
tr: Going the wrong way for a unit in the denominator
Leaving the answer in miles per minute

tm.nm: Square or cube the factor (area, volume, per second squared)
tl: square inches, square feet, square meters per minute, meters per second squared
only a length factor is given (1 foot = 12 inches)
tm.ask: the amount in the new squared or cubed unit
tm.rl: Square (or cube) the length factor; square the time factor for “per second squared”.
hd: 1 square foot = 12² = 144 square inches.
Convert time separately; for “per second squared” use 60².
tr: Using the length factor without squaring
Squaring the time factor only once (or not at all)
Forgetting the time conversion

tm.nm: Rate × time = amount (and its reverses)
tl: a constant rate or unit price
one of amount, rate, time given with another
Easy
tm.ask: the amount, the time, or the unit rate
tm.rl: Amount = rate × time; time = amount ÷ rate; rate = amount ÷ time.
hd: Write amount = rate × time with the numbers in place.
Solve for the missing one.
tr: Adding or subtracting the two numbers
Answering the rate itself

tm.nm: Density of a cube: mass = density × edge³
tl: “density … kilograms per cubic meter”
a cube with its edge length
“to the nearest whole number / hundredth”
tm.ask: the mass, the edge length or the density
tm.rl: Volume = edge³ first; then mass = density × volume.
hd: Cube the edge: 0.6³ = 0.216.
Mass = density × volume; edge = ∛(mass ÷ density); density = mass ÷ edge³.
tr: Forgetting to cube the edge
Dividing the wrong way
Forgetting the cube root

tm.nm: Density = amount ÷ area (or volume)
tl: population per square mile, grams per cubic centimeter, square feet per person
a total and a size
tm.ask: the density, the size, the count, or a change
tm.rl: Density = amount ÷ size; build the right size first (land area = total − water).
hd: Write density = amount ÷ size.
Use only the size the unit names (“per square mile of land area”).
Solve for the missing piece.
tr: Dividing by the total area instead of the land area
The four operations as choices (N/V, N − V, N + V, N × V)
Answering the new total instead of the increase

tm.nm: Ratios and proportions: find the missing number
tl: “the ratio of m to k is 1 to 5”, “proportional relationship”
one value of the pair given
tm.ask: the other quantity, a factor or a change
tm.rl: Set up a/b = c/d in the stated order, or scale both parts by the same factor.
hd: Write the ratio in the order stated.
Find the scale factor from the known part; multiply the other part by it.
Changes keep the same ratio as the quantities.
tr: Reversing the ratio
Adding instead of scaling (3 + 3 = 6)
Using a decoy number in the ratio

tm.nm: Proportional expressions with letters
tl: “the total mass of r objects is t”, “87 millimeters every m months”
choices are expressions in letters
tm.ask: an expression for a scaled amount, time or length
tm.rl: Plug in easy numbers (m = 12, k = 1) and test the choices.
ds: Define m=12, k=1 and evaluate each choice
hd: Scale the count and the total by the same factor (146r → 146t).
Or plug in numbers that make the story easy and test each choice.
tr: Dividing by 12 instead of multiplying (years to months)
Adding a factor of 12 that the scale already includes
Answering for the other object

tm.nm: Difference of two multiples: factor first
tl: two rates or fractions of the same base
“how many more …”
tm.ask: the difference
tm.rl: Subtract the rates first, then multiply once.
tr: Answering one of the two totals

tm.nm: Substitute a ratio as a block
tl: x/y = 4 given
a second equation containing x/y with other factors
tm.ask: the unknown n
tm.rl: Replace x/y (or a/b) by its value, then solve.
tr: Trying to find x and y separately

tm.nm: Doubling each year: work backward
tl: “doubled each year until … $480 on January 1, 2005”
tm.ask: the starting amount
tm.rl: Count the doublings (2001 to 2005 is 4), divide by 2 that many times.
tr: Counting 5 doublings

tm.nm: Convert currency, then take off a fee
tl: an exchange rate and a percent fee
tm.ask: the amount received
tm.rl: Convert, then multiply by (1 − fee).
tr: Skipping the fee

tm.nm: Scale a sample up to a population
tl: k of n sampled customers
“best estimate of the total”
tm.ask: estimated count
tr: Powers-of-ten slips

tm.nm: Compare two unit rates
tl: a table of grams and costs for two foods
“ratio of the cost per gram …”
tm.ask: a ratio of unit rates
tm.rl: Find each unit rate, then their ratio.
tr: Ratio of the protein amounts
Ratio reversed

tm.nm: Similar squares share a total by area
tl: two squares, one with sides 3 times the other
a total split in proportion to area
tm.ask: the larger square’s share
tm.rl: Side ratio 3 → area ratio 9: the larger gets 9/10 of the total.
hd: Area ratio = 3² = 9 to 1.
Larger share = 9/10 of the total.
tr: Splitting 3 to 1

tm.nm: p% of a number
tl: “what is p% of N”, “p% of the … were …”
one whole and one percent
mostly Easy
tm.ask: the part
tm.rl: Part = (p/100) × whole; Desmos for tiny or odd percents.
ds: 0.001/100*140 (type the percent over 100 exactly as printed)
hd: Move the decimal two places: p% = p/100.
Multiply by the whole; convert units if the answer asks for different ones.
tr: Tiny percents: 0.001% is 0.00001, not 0.001
Forgetting a unit change (hours to minutes)
Off-by-one period count (“the next 5 months” plus the first)

tm.nm: What percent is the part of the whole?
tl: two counts given
“p% of …, what is p”, “what percent of A’s calls …”
tm.ask: a percent
tm.rl: Part ÷ whole × 100; the whole follows “of”.
hd: The number after “of” is the whole.
Percent = part ÷ whole × 100.
tr: Dividing by the wrong total (grand total instead of the row)
The complement percent

tm.nm: Increase or decrease by p%: the new value or expression
tl: “increase by p%”, “decrease by p%”
choices like 1.43w, 0.57w, 0.43w
tm.ask: the new amount
tm.rl: Multiply by (1 + p/100) or (1 − p/100).
hd: Increase: × (1 + p/100); decrease: × (1 − p/100).
tr: Adding p as an amount (113,000 + 29)
Only the change (0.43w) instead of the new amount

tm.nm: Find the original (the whole) from a part or an after-value
tl: the value after the change, or the part, is given
“how many were there before”, “how many in total”, “how many were removed”
tm.ask: the original whole
tm.rl: Divide by the multiplier; never multiply the after-value by the percent.
hd: After = original × multiplier, so original = after ÷ multiplier (99 ÷ 1.125 = 88).
Part = p% of whole, so whole = part ÷ (p/100).
For “how many were removed”, subtract after from original.
tr: Applying the percent to the after-value (0.8 × 88)
Answering the original when asked for the amount removed
Using 4 instead of 5 for “400% greater”

tm.nm: Percent change from two values
tl: an old and a new value (maybe read from a graph)
“percent decrease”, “p% greater than”, “p% of the other”
tm.ask: p
tm.rl: Change ÷ original × 100; “A is p% of B” is A ÷ B × 100.
hd: p = (new − old) ÷ old × 100.
For “B is p% of A” when A = 1.27B: p = 100 ÷ 1.27.
tr: Dividing by the new value
The ratio as the percent (700 instead of 600)
Entering 0.75 for 75

tm.nm: Translate between a multiplier and a percent change
tl: “new = k × old” or an expression like 0.35x
“increased by 131%”, “decreased by what percent”
tm.ask: the multiplier k, or the percent it means
tm.rl: k = 1 ± p/100; a multiplier below 1 means a decrease of (1 − k) × 100%.
hd: 0.35x is a 65% decrease, not 35%.
tr: Answering the multiplier as the percent (35%)
1.31 for an increase of 131%

tm.nm: Chained percent changes: multiply the multipliers
tl: two or more percent changes in a row (“70% less than b … 60% greater than a”)
“how many times b”, “net percent increase”, one dollar value given
tm.ask: the overall multiplier, net change or one of the values
tm.rl: Write each step as a multiplier and multiply; divide when going back to the base.
hd: Convert each step: 70% less → 0.3, 60% greater → 1.6, “290% of” → 2.9.
Multiply in order; if the known value is at the end of the chain, divide back.
tr: Adding the percents (−70% + 60% = −10%)
Going the wrong direction in the chain (2.34 × 0.7 instead of ÷ 1.3)

tm.nm: Percent-of chains and nested subgroups
tl: “a is 2,241% of …, b is 83% of c”
“of those, 37% are …”
huge or tiny percents
tm.ask: a percent or expression linking two variables, or a nested count
tm.rl: Plug in c = 1 (or 100) in Desmos and let it carry the decimals.
hd: Convert each percent to a decimal carefully (0.008% = 0.00008).
Express everything in one variable, then form the ratio and × 100.
tr: Missing the × 100 (49.41% instead of 4,941%)
Tiny-percent decimal slip
Answering the subgroup instead of “not” the subgroup

tm.nm: Repeated percent of the previous value
tl: “depreciate by 20% of the previous year’s value”
tm.ask: value after t periods
tm.rl: Multiply by (1 − p/100) once per period.
tr: The linear version: 20% of the original each year

tm.nm: Next change as a multiple of the last percent change
tl: a table of two years
“the percent increase … would be double …”
tm.ask: projected value
tm.rl: Find the first percent change, scale it as stated, apply it.
hd: Next increase is half of that, 2.5%: 5,880 × 1.025.
tr: Doubling instead of halving (reversed wording)
Adding the same amount instead of the percent

tm.nm: Enlarged drawing: distance per inch
tl: a scale drawing enlarged by p%
“1 inch represents … miles”
tm.ask: miles per inch on the larger drawing
tm.rl: Larger drawing, fewer miles per inch: divide by the multiplier.
tr: Multiplying by 1.65

tm.nm: Percent of a daily allowance from x servings
tl: “each serving … is 5% of the daily allowance”
p percent from x servings
tm.ask: p in terms of x
tm.rl: p is already in percent units: p = 5x.
hd: Each serving adds 5 percentage points: p = 5x.
tr: Exponential forms (1.05)^x
Dividing by 100 (0.05x)

tm.nm: Read a bar graph or frequency table
tl: a bar graph or frequency table
“how many …”, “how many more … than …”, “minimum value”, “which table represents the list”
Easy
tm.ask: a frequency, a difference of two frequencies, or a data value
tm.rl: No calculation beyond one subtraction.
hd: Find the bar or row named in the question and read its height or count.
For “how many more”, subtract the two bars.
“Minimum value” comes from the Value column, not the smallest frequency.
tr: The smallest frequency given as the minimum value
Reading the wrong bar or adding instead of subtracting

tm.nm: Find the mean of a list or table
tl: a short list, table or bar graph
“what is the mean …”
tm.ask: the mean
tm.rl: Desmos mean() is fastest for long lists; a frequency table needs total(V*F)/total(F).
ds: frequency table: V=[…], F=[…], total(V*F)/total(F)
hd: Add the values (each times its frequency) and divide by how many there are.
tr: Dividing by the number of rows instead of the total frequency

tm.nm: Find the median of a list, table or box plot
tl: “median”
a list (maybe unsorted), a frequency table or a box plot
tm.ask: the median
tm.rl: Sort first; for a box plot read the middle line.
ds: median([…])
frequency table: median of the expanded list, e.g. median(join(L1,L2…)) or count to the middle position
hd: Sort the values.
Middle position (n + 1)/2; for an even count, average the two middle values.
Box plot: the line inside the box.
tr: The unsorted middle value
A quartile (box edge) instead of the median
The mean instead of the median

tm.nm: Which bin holds the median?
tl: counts of values in intervals (2 to 7, 8 to 13, …)
“which could be the median”
tm.ask: a possible median
tm.rl: Count to the middle position through the bins.
hd: Middle position = (n + 1)/2.
Add the bin counts until you pass that position; that bin holds the median.
Pick the choice inside that bin.
tr: Picking the bin with the most values

tm.nm: Range (max − min), including box plots
tl: “range”
a list, table or two box plots
tm.ask: a range or the difference of two ranges
tm.rl: Hand: largest minus smallest.
hd: Range = maximum − minimum (whisker end to whisker end on a box plot).
For two box plots, find each range, then subtract.
tr: Subtracting box widths (IQRs), medians or maximums
Half-values from misidentifying max or min

tm.nm: Add or remove one extreme value: what happens to the mean and median?
tl: a value far outside the data is added or removed
choices pair “mean greater/less” with “median greater/equal”
tm.ask: how the mean and median change
tm.rl: The mean always moves toward the new value; the median moves at most one half-step and often not at all.
ds: Optional: V=[…], F=[…], compare total(V*F)/total(F) before and after; median of the expanded list
hd: Mean: moves toward the added value (away from a removed one).
Median: find the middle position before and after; if both land in the same repeated value, it is unchanged.
tr: Assuming the median moves with the mean
Moving the mean the wrong way

tm.nm: Shift or stretch every value: which statistic changes?
tl: “adding 56 to each value”, “adding 7 to each number above the median and subtracting 7 below”
“which measure does NOT stay the same”
tm.ask: which statistics change
tm.rl: Adding k to every value moves the center by k and keeps the spread; pushing values apart keeps the median but raises the standard deviation.
hd: Same amount added to all: mean and median +k, range and standard deviation unchanged.
Values pushed away from the middle: median and (if balanced) mean unchanged; standard deviation larger.
tr: Thinking the range changes when every value shifts
Thinking the median changes

tm.nm: Combined mean of two groups
tl: two groups with their sizes and means
“mean of the combined …”
tm.ask: the combined (weighted) mean
tm.rl: Total of all values ÷ total count, never the average of the two means.
hd: Total = n₁·mean₁ + n₂·mean₂.
Divide by n₁ + n₂.
tr: Averaging the two means

tm.nm: Find a missing value from the mean (sum = count × mean)
tl: a mean before and after a value is removed or added, or two data sets with related means
one unknown value x
tm.ask: the missing or removed value
tm.rl: Work with sums: sum = count × mean.
ds: Optional: (sum of the other values + x)/n = mean, let Desmos draw x
hd: Old sum = n × old mean; new sum = (n − 1) × new mean.
The missing value is the difference of the sums (or solve sum + x = n × mean).
tr: Forgetting the count drops by one (dividing by 20 again)
Subtracting the means

tm.nm: Compare the centers of two data sets
tl: two lists, two frequency columns or two histograms
“which statement compares the means/medians”, “how much greater”
tm.ask: which center is larger, or by how much
tm.rl: Compare totals with the same count; use symmetry or a plug-in (a = 1) for symbolic tables.
ds: V=[…], A=[…], B=[…]; total(V*A)/total(A) and total(V*B)/total(B)
hd: Same count: the larger sum has the larger mean.
Reversed frequencies over evenly spaced values: the side weighted toward big values has the bigger mean.
For medians, count to the middle position in each set.
tr: Comparing frequencies instead of values
“Not enough information” when the table is enough

tm.nm: Standard deviation and skew: compare without computing
tl: two dot plots or histograms of the same shape
“compare the standard deviations”, “mean greater than the median”, “order the mean, median and mode”
tm.ask: which set is more spread out, or how the mean and median compare
tm.rl: Spread = distance from the center, not bar heights; a long right tail pulls the mean above the median; symmetric data have mean = median.
ds: stdevp(L) for each set when a comparison is close
hd: Same shape shifted: same standard deviation.
More values far from the center: larger standard deviation.
Tail to the right: mode < median < mean. Symmetric: mean = median (plug in a = 1 if the table uses a).
tr: Comparing bar heights or counts instead of distance from the mean
Thinking a shift changes the standard deviation

tm.nm: What a summary can or cannot tell you
tl: box plots, or only a total and a count
“which must be true”, “which can be calculated”, “which is NOT equal to k”
tm.ask: which statistic is known or true
tm.rl: Box plots give only min, quartiles, median and max: never the mean.
hd: Strike any choice about a statistic the display does not show (means from box plots).
Check the rest directly against the numbers.
tr: Choosing a mean comparison from box plots

tm.nm: Unknown values from the mean, median and range together
tl: an ordered list with letters
mean, median and range all given
tm.ask: one unknown value
tm.rl: Median fixes the middle letter; mean gives a sum; range gives max − min.
hd: Median = the middle value, so b = 29.
Sum = 7 × 36 gives a + c; range gives c − a; solve.
tr: Answering the range itself (72)

tm.nm: Estimate the slope of the line of best fit
tl: a line of best fit is drawn
“closest to the slope” or “predicted increase in y for every increase of 1 in x”
decimal choices
tm.ask: the slope, read from the graph
tm.rl: Hand: two lattice points on the line, rise over run.
ds: Optional: y=mx+b with a slider for m, matched to the drawn line
hd: Pick two points where the line crosses gridlines, far apart.
Slope = change in y ÷ change in x; check the sign (falling = negative).
Read axis labels, not gridline counts (labels may go up by 2).
tr: Counting gridlines when labels go up by 2 or 10
Wrong sign for a falling line

tm.nm: Read the model’s value at a given x
tl: a line or curve drawn through data (or a clear trend)
“according to the model, … when x = k”
choices spaced far apart
tm.ask: predicted y at x = k (or a difference of two such values)
tm.rl: Hand: go up from x = k to the model, then across.
hd: Go up from x = k to the line or curve (not to a dot).
Read across to the y-axis; for a difference, read both values and subtract.
tr: Reading the nearest data point instead of the model
f(50) − f(30) computed as f(20) for a curve
Answering an x-value

tm.nm: Which equation is the line? (signs of slope and intercept)
tl: choices differ only in the signs of the slope and intercept (or one has a different sign)
Easy or Medium
tm.ask: the line’s equation
tm.rl: Hand: sign of the slope from the direction, sign of the intercept from where it meets the y-axis.
ds: Optional: table of the points, y_1~mx_1+b
hd: Rising = positive slope, falling = negative.
Meets the y-axis above 0 = positive intercept.
Watch y = a + bx order: the number with x is the slope.
tr: Reading y = a + bx as if the first number were the slope

tm.nm: Which equation is the line? (intercept hidden by a cut-off axis)
tl: choices share a slope or intercept and differ in the other value
axes that do not start at 0
tm.ask: the line’s equation
tm.rl: Hand: slope from two points, then b = y − mx; the corner of a cut-off graph is not the intercept.
ds: Graph the choices with the window set to the graph’s axes and see which runs along the line
hd: Slope from two points on the line.
Intercept b = y − m·x from one point (do not read it off a truncated axis).
tr: Using the corner value (300) of a truncated axis as the intercept

tm.nm: Linear or exponential, increasing or decreasing
tl: choices: increasing/decreasing × linear/exponential
a situation in words, a graph or tables
tm.ask: the kind of function
tm.rl: Same amount each step = linear; same percent or factor = exponential; then the direction.
hd: Constant amount per step (or constant y-differences) = linear.
Constant percent or factor (constant ratios) = exponential.
Then rising or falling.
tr: “201% of x” read as exponential: a fixed multiple of x is linear
“rate of 400 feet per minute” read as exponential

tm.nm: Read a graph: the highest point, a value, a point
tl: a line graph or scatterplot in context
“in which year … greatest”, “how many … for the 50-pound wolf”, “which statement is NOT true”
tm.ask: a value, a point or a true statement read from the graph
tm.rl: No calculation.
hd: Find the point or peak asked about and read the other coordinate.
For NOT-true questions, check each statement against the graph.
tr: The year after the peak
Counting a flat segment as increasing or decreasing

tm.nm: Average rate of change between two given x-values
tl: “average rate of change … from … to …”
a graph or scatterplot; x may be “days after January 11”
tm.ask: change in y ÷ change in x
tm.rl: Hand: translate the given dates into x first.
hd: Turn each date into its x-value (January 13 = 2 days after January 11).
Read both y-values; divide the change in y by the change in x.
tr: Using the calendar dates as x

tm.nm: Which interval changes the most?
tl: equal-length intervals as choices
“greatest increase/decrease”, “greatest average rate”
tm.ask: the interval with the biggest change
tm.rl: Equal widths: compare the vertical changes only.
hd: For each interval read the start and end values.
Biggest difference wins (steepest segment).

tm.nm: Pick the curved model (quadratic or exponential)
tl: a U shape, an arch or a decaying curve
choices that differ in signs or in a base b
tm.ask: the model equation, its base or its graph
tm.rl: Hand: shape gives the sign of a (or 0 < b < 1 for decay); the y-intercept gives the constant.
ds: Table of read-off points, then y_1~ax_1^2+bx_1+c or y_1~ab^{x_1}
hd: Opens up: a > 0; arch: a < 0. Decay: 0 < b < 1.
Where the trend meets the y-axis gives the constant term.
For graph choices, keep the one with the right shape and points on both sides.
tr: Picking the y-intercept value as b
A curve of the right shape that misses the data

tm.nm: Residuals: actual versus predicted
tl: “predict a greater y-value than the actual”
“difference between the data point and the predicted value”
tm.ask: a residual or a count of points above or below the line
tm.rl: Predicted greater than actual = point below the line.
hd: Translate: actual > predicted means above the line; predicted > actual means below.
Count those points, or subtract the line’s value from the point’s value.
tr: Counting the points on the wrong side
Reading values from an axis that starts at 6, not 0

tm.nm: Meaning of the slope of the line of best fit
tl: an equation or a drawn line of best fit in context
“best interpretation of the slope”, “predicted increase for an increase of 5”
choices mix the right number with the wrong unit (per year / per 10 years)
tm.ask: what the slope means, or slope × a change in x
tm.rl: Slope = change in y for each 1 unit of x, in the units of the axes.
hd: Name y and x with their units.
Slope says: y changes by m for each 1 unit of x (scale it: m × 5 for 5 units).
Reject choices with the variables swapped or the wrong time step.
tr: Per 10 years because the data are plotted every 10 years
Answering the slope (57) when asked for the change over 5 units
The intercept instead of the slope

tm.nm: Exponential eventually overtakes linear
tl: a percent growth and a fixed-amount growth (or 2^x and 2x + 2)
choices: always more, always less, more at first then less, …
tm.ask: how the two compare over time
tm.rl: An increasing exponential eventually passes any linear function; compare the first step.
ds: y=2^x {x>0} and y=2x+2 {x>0}; click the intersection
hd: Compare at the start (x = 1).
Exponential growth keeps increasing its step, so it ends up ahead.
tr: Comparing balances instead of amounts earned per year

tm.nm: Every y multiplied by k: the new line of best fit
tl: “created by multiplying the y-coordinate of each data point by 3.9”
tm.ask: the new line’s equation
tm.rl: Multiply both the slope and the intercept by k.
hd: Read the old line: intercept 12, slope 1.5.
Multiply both by 3.9.
tr: Scaling only the slope or only the intercept

tm.nm: Mean of the y-values for a range of x
tl: a scatterplot of items
“average … for boards wider than 18 and narrower than 48”
tm.ask: a mean of selected points
tm.rl: List the points in the range (watch stacked dots), then average.
hd: List the y-values whose x is in range.
Add and divide by how many.
tr: Missing one of two stacked dots

tm.nm: One group, no condition: count ÷ total
tl: “selected at random” with no “given”, “of those” or “if … is”
counts in the text, a one-way table or a short list
choices in fraction, decimal or n/(n + k) form
tm.ask: probability of one category
tm.rl: Denominator: everything that could be picked.
ds: k/N (Desmos prints the decimal when the choices are decimals)
hd: Count the wanted outcome.
Divide by the total number of outcomes (add the table’s rows if there is no total).
Check place value: 4/1000 = 0.004.
tr: Part-to-part ratio (n/12 instead of n/(n + 12))
Place value (0.04 instead of 0.004)
A choice greater than 1
The complement category’s count

tm.nm: Count the qualifying outcomes first (neither, both, a range)
tl: “neither … nor …”, “even and at most 50”
counts or a range of integers to count from
tm.ask: probability of an event built from two conditions
tm.rl: Denominator: the whole set. Do the counting before dividing.
ds: L=[1...160] | length(L[mod(L,2)=0 and L<=50]) (Desmos: L[mod(L,2)=0] then filter again)
hd: Turn the event into a count: neither blue nor yellow = red + white.
Divide by the whole set and reduce.
tr: Dividing by only the other categories (7/11)
Dropping one condition (all integers ≤ 50)

tm.nm: Two-way table, no condition: row or column total ÷ grand total
tl: a two-way table with totals
“selected at random” and one feature, no “given”
tm.ask: probability of one row or column
tm.rl: Denominator: the grand total.
hd: Find the row or column total for the feature.
Divide by the grand total.
tr: The other marginal totals

tm.nm: Two-way table, both features: one cell ÷ grand total
tl: two features joined by “and” or “has … and does not have …”
often no totals printed
tm.ask: probability of one cell
tm.rl: Denominator: the grand total (add all cells if no total is printed).
hd: Find the one cell with both features.
Add every cell for the denominator.
tr: A row or column total as the denominator (the conditional versions)

tm.nm: Two-way table, “given that” / “of those”: cell ÷ that row or column
tl: “given that”, “of the … that”, “if a … is selected from those who …”
a two-way table
tm.ask: conditional probability or percent
tm.rl: Denominator: the total of the group after “given that” / “of those”, never the grand total.
ds: cell/(row or column total) (only to convert to a decimal or percent)
hd: Circle the group named after “given” or “of those”: its total is the denominator.
The numerator is the cell inside that group with the feature asked.
Give the form asked (fraction, decimal, percent).
tr: Grand total as the denominator
Condition reversed (the other margin as the denominator)

tm.nm: Conditional probability over combined rows or columns
tl: “at least”, “greater than”, “not in group 2” inside the condition
the condition covers two or more rows or columns
one-way table of ranges or percents
tm.ask: conditional probability where the condition is a union
tm.rl: Denominator: the sum of every row or column the condition covers (or 100% minus the excluded ones).
ds: (cells)/(sum of covered totals), e.g. 0.24/(1-0.26)
hd: List the rows or columns the condition covers; add their totals for the denominator.
Add the wanted cells inside them for the numerator.
With percents, use 100% minus the excluded rows as the denominator.
tr: Using only one of the covered columns
Condition reversed
Forgetting the excluded row (using 100%)

tm.nm: Conditional probability from counts described in words
tl: rows of trees, boxes of items: counts given as groups × per group
“given that”
tm.ask: conditional probability
tm.rl: Build the hidden two-way table first.
hd: Multiply out each count (rows × per row).
Denominator: total of the given group; numerator: the wanted part of it.
tr: Using per-row counts and ignoring the different numbers of rows

tm.nm: Probability given, find a count
tl: “the probability … is 0.35” (or two probabilities)
“how many …”
tm.ask: a count from a probability
tm.rl: Count = probability × total; for the last category subtract the others from 1 first.
hd: If needed, P(last) = 1 − the others.
Multiply by the total.
tr: Answering the percent (28) instead of the count (98)
Using the old total (83 million) instead of the stated one

tm.nm: Conditional probability given, solve for a missing cell
tl: a two-way table with x in one cell
“the probability … given … is 1/9”
tm.ask: the unknown cell
tm.rl: Write cell ÷ (group total with x) = given probability.
ds: 2/(10+x)=1/9 → Desmos draws x = 8
hd: Scale the fraction: 1/9 = 2/18, so the group total is 18 = 10 + x.

tm.nm: Two-way table arithmetic (no probability)
tl: a two-way table with a missing cell, or “closest to 1/3 of …”
filed under probability but asks for a count or a category
tm.ask: a count or a category from the table
tm.rl: Plain table arithmetic.
hd: Missing cell: the known total minus the known cells.
Closest fraction: compute the target (180 ÷ 3 = 60) and scan the column.
tr: Using the grand total instead of the column total

tm.nm: Rate × time as a fraction of a total (no probability)
tl: “every day” rate
“what fraction of the first 60,000 …”
tm.ask: a fraction
tm.rl: Rate × time ÷ total.

tm.nm: Margin of error: the plausible interval
tl: an estimate “with an associated margin of error of …”
choices about the population, using “plausible”, “between”, “exactly”
sometimes a two-way table to compute the estimate from
tm.ask: the conclusion that uses estimate ± margin for the sampled population
tm.rl: Hand: two subtractions, then a wording check.
hd: Interval = estimate − margin to estimate + margin.
Keep only choices about the population that was sampled.
Pick “plausible … between” the two ends; reject “exactly”, “not possible” and anything about other groups.
tr: Treating the estimate as exact (“is 38%”)
A conclusion about a wider group than the one sampled
Using the sample size as a count in the interval
“Not possible” instead of “doubtful” for a value just outside the interval

tm.nm: Scale a sample up to the population
tl: “selected at random”, k of n in the sample have a trait
a population total N is given
“best estimate of the number …”
tm.ask: estimated count in the population
tm.rl: Hand, or Desmos as a calculator; with a list of values, Desmos mean().
ds: N*k/n (for a list of sample values: L=[…], then mean(L)*N)
hd: Sample share = k ÷ n (or 1 − share for “fewer than”).
Estimate = share × N. Pick “best estimate”, never “exactly … must”.
tr: Dividing N by k instead of multiplying by k/n
Answering the complement group (at least two vs fewer than two siblings)
Using the min, median or max instead of the mean
Reporting the sample difference without scaling it up

tm.nm: Margin of error on a percent, as a count
tl: a percent estimate with a margin of error
a population size (10,000 beads, 50,000 people)
choices are counts or inequalities in counts
tm.ask: plausible count in the population
tm.rl: Hand: two multiplications.
hd: Percent interval: p − m to p + m.
Multiply both ends by the population size (not the sample size).
tr: Multiplying by the sample size
Using the complement percent

tm.nm: Bigger sample, smaller margin of error
tl: two samples or a planned larger sample
“effect on the margin of error” or “reason the margin of error is greater”
tm.ask: how sample size and margin of error move together
tm.rl: No calculation: larger random sample, smaller margin; the estimate itself does not move predictably.
hd: Larger sample → smaller margin of error.
Larger margin → the sample was smaller.
tr: Thinking the estimate itself goes up or down
Linking the margin to the percent in favor

tm.nm: Find the margin of error from the interval
tl: an estimate and an interval are given
“what is the margin of error”
tm.ask: the margin of error
tm.rl: Hand: one subtraction.
hd: Margin = estimate − lower end (or half the interval’s width).
tr: Taking the full width of the interval

tm.nm: Which conclusion the sample supports
tl: a random sample of one kind (largemouth bass)
choices about all fish versus that kind
tm.ask: conclusion limited to the sampled kind
tm.rl: No calculation: keep the sampled group and the sample percent.
hd: Match the choice’s group to the group sampled.
Keep the sample’s percent as an estimate.

tm.nm: Largest population the results apply to
tl: “largest population to which the results can be generalized”
“selected at random from …”
a table or result that plays no role
tm.ask: the widest group the sample represents
tm.rl: No calculation: copy the group after “selected at random from”, with every qualifier.
hd: Find the sentence with “at random from”.
Keep every qualifier in it (grade, school, region, age, year).
Pick the choice with exactly those qualifiers: not the sample itself, nothing wider.
tr: A wider group that drops one qualifier (another grade, the whole county)
The sample itself (“the 40 students surveyed”)
A number changed by the study length (17-year-old trees become 19)

tm.nm: Why the sample is biased
tl: survey taken at one special place or only from one subgroup (dog owners, a playground)
or viewers who chose to answer (a website poll)
“must be true” / “best explanation”
tm.ask: the statement that says the sample is not representative
tm.rl: No calculation: compare who was asked with who the claim is about.
hd: Name the population the claim is about.
Name who was actually asked and how they got in the sample.
If they are a special subgroup or volunteered, pick “biased / not a random sample”.
tr: A bigger sample of the same subgroup (“survey more dog owners”) does not fix bias
Blaming the sample size instead of the method
Percentages that do not add to 100% (a decoy)

tm.nm: A sample percent is not an exact population percent
tl: a random sample with p% saying yes
Roman-numeral statements claiming “exactly p%” for the population or another sample
“must be true”
tm.ask: which statements must be true
tm.rl: No exact-percent claim about the population or a new sample must hold: answer “none”.
hd: Each statement claims an exact percent beyond the sample.
Samples vary, so none must be true: choose “Neither” / “None”.
tr: Treating the sample percent as the population percent

tm.nm: Which conclusion the sample allows
tl: sample drawn from people who already share a trait (“liked the book”)
“which inference can appropriately be drawn”
tm.ask: the conclusion limited to the sampled group
tm.rl: Pick the choice about the sampled group, worded loosely (“most”).
hd: Name the group sampled from.
Reject choices about wider or opposite groups.
Prefer the hedged choice (“most”) over the exact 95%.
tr: Exact sample percent applied to everyone who sees movies or reads books

tm.nm: Area formula: plug in the dimensions
tl: a rectangle, triangle, circle or parallelogram with every dimension given
Easy
tm.ask: the area (or an expression for it)
tm.rl: Use the reference-sheet formula; the triangle needs the ½.
hd: Rectangle lw; triangle ½bh; circle πr²; parallelogram bh.
For “k longer than”, build the second side first.
tr: Forgetting the ½ for a triangle
Using the diameter as the radius

tm.nm: Area known: solve for a dimension
tl: the area and one dimension given
or two figures with equal area
tm.ask: the missing side, base or height
tm.rl: Write the formula with the area filled in, then solve.
hd: Area = formula; put in what you know.
Solve for the missing length (equal areas: set the two formulas equal).
tr: Dropping the ½ for a triangle (answering 18 instead of 36)

tm.nm: Add or subtract piece areas
tl: two separate shapes, or a shape with a part removed
“total area”, “area of the shaded region”
tm.ask: a combined area
tm.rl: Find each piece’s area, then add or subtract.
hd: Area of each piece (get a radius from an area if needed).
Add for “total”, subtract for “remaining”.
tr: Adding radii instead of areas

tm.nm: Circle: radius, diameter, circumference, area
tl: one circle measure given (circumference 31π, area 100π)
“what is the diameter/radius”
tm.ask: another circle measure
tm.rl: C = πd = 2πr; A = πr².
hd: Circumference 31π means d = 31.
Area kπ means r = √k.
tr: Giving the radius when the diameter is asked

tm.nm: Areas that need the distance formula or the hypotenuse
tl: vertices plotted in the xy-plane, sides not along the gridlines
three side lengths with radicals (right angle not marked)
tm.ask: an area, a leg, or a circle’s circumference through three points
tm.rl: Distance formula for slanted sides; box-and-subtract (or the shoelace formula) for a slanted triangle.
ds: Polygon: type polygon((-3,4),(5,3),(4,-3)) and read its area in the list
hd: Slanted side length = √(Δx² + Δy²).
Rectangle area = product of two adjacent sides; triangle: enclose it in a box and subtract the corner triangles.
Right triangle: the longest side is the hypotenuse; area = ½ × the two legs.
tr: Multiplying the hypotenuse by a leg
Counting grid squares along a slanted side

tm.nm: Perimeter: add the sides
tl: side lengths of a polygon
“perimeter”
Easy
tm.ask: the perimeter or a missing side
tm.rl: Add every side; for a missing side subtract the known sides from the perimeter.
hd: Perimeter = sum of all sides (square: 4s).
Missing side = perimeter − the other sides.
tr: Adding only the labeled sides

tm.nm: Scale factor: lengths × k, areas × k², volumes × k³
tl: “similar”, “each side 41 times”, “length and width each increased by 20%”
an area or volume ratio given or asked
tm.ask: an area factor, a length, a perimeter or a volume
tm.rl: Length factor k ↔ area factor k² ↔ volume factor k³; go back with √ or ∛.
hd: Find k from a pair of lengths (or √ of the area ratio, ∛ of the volume ratio).
Areas: × k²; volumes: × k³; perimeters and edges: × k.
tr: Using k for an area (41 instead of 1,681)
Using the area ratio for a perimeter
Adding 20% to the area instead of 1.2²

tm.nm: Similar figures: perimeters and sides scale by the same k
tl: two similar triangles or polygons
perimeters and one side given
tm.ask: a side or a perimeter
tm.rl: Perimeter ratio = side ratio.
hd: k = one perimeter ÷ the other (or side ÷ side).
Multiply the known side or perimeter by k.
tr: Inverting k

tm.nm: Volume formula: plug in (prism, cylinder, sphere, cone, pyramid)
tl: a solid with its dimensions (or a diameter, circumference or percent change to the radius)
“volume … in terms of π”, “n π”
tm.ask: the volume
tm.rl: Reference-sheet formula; get the radius first; cones and pyramids take ⅓.
ds: (1/3)*pi*9^2*22/pi (or (2/3)*pi*27^3 for a hemisphere)
hd: Radius first (half the diameter; 1.25 × 16 for “25% longer”).
Prism lwh; cylinder πr²h; cone and pyramid ⅓ × base × h; sphere (4/3)πr³ (half for a hemisphere).
tr: Using the diameter as the radius
Forgetting the ⅓ or the ½ for a hemisphere

tm.nm: Volume known: solve for a dimension
tl: the volume and all but one dimension
“length of an edge of the base”, “radius of the base”
tm.ask: the missing dimension or base area
tm.rl: Put the volume into the formula and solve; take the square or cube root at the end.
ds: 14x^2=2016 → Desmos draws x = 12 (use the positive one)
hd: Volume = formula with the known pieces.
Divide, then take the root for a squared or cubed dimension.
tr: Forgetting the square root (answering the base area)
Forgetting the ⅓ for a cone

tm.nm: Leftover volume: outer − inner
tl: a sphere inside a cube, fruit and syrup in a can
“not taken up by”, “volume of the fruit”
tm.ask: the leftover volume
tm.rl: Outer volume − inner (or filled) volume.
hd: Compute the container’s volume.
Subtract the part that is something else.
tr: Answering the container’s full volume

tm.nm: Radius and height scaled differently
tl: “twice the radius and half the height”
“392 times as large”
tm.ask: the new volume or the factor pair
tm.rl: Cylinder or cone volume factor = (radius factor)² × (height factor).
hd: Square the radius factor, multiply by the height factor.
Test each choice: 7² × 8 = 392.
tr: Not squaring the radius factor

tm.nm: Cube: edge, surface area and volume
tl: a cube with one of edge, surface area or volume
tm.ask: another of the three
tm.rl: Surface area 6s², volume s³.
hd: From surface area: s² = SA ÷ 6.
Volume = s³.
tr: Dividing the surface area by 6 and stopping

tm.nm: Surface area of a box (with missing or glued faces)
tl: a rectangular prism or cube
“surface area”, “does not have a lid”, “glued together along a base”
tm.ask: the surface area, an expression, or a dimension
tm.rl: 2(lw + lh + wh); remove missing faces; gluing removes two faces.
hd: Add the areas of all six faces: 2(lw + lh + wh).
No lid: five faces. Glued: 2 × one prism − 2 × the glued face.
tr: Counting six faces for an open box
Subtracting only one glued face

tm.nm: Cone or pyramid: slant height by Pythagoras
tl: a right cone or pyramid
volume and base area, or the slant height asked
tm.ask: the slant height or a dimension
tm.rl: Height from the volume; slant² = r² + h².
hd: r from the base area; h = 3V ÷ base area.
Slant height = √(r² + h²).
tr: Answering the height instead of the slant height

tm.nm: Parallel lines and a transversal: equal or supplementary
tl: “line m is parallel to line n”
one angle given (a number or an expression in k)
mostly Easy
tm.ask: another angle or the variable
tm.rl: Every acute angle is equal; every obtuse angle is equal; an acute and an obtuse angle add to 180.
hd: Decide whether the two angles look alike (both acute or both obtuse): equal.
Otherwise they add to 180.
With expressions, set them equal (or to 180), solve, then answer the angle asked.
tr: Answering the equal angle when the asked one is supplementary
Stopping at k instead of the angle

tm.nm: Sums of angles written with x: which sum is (not) possible
tl: “forming four acute angles and four obtuse angles” (or two of each)
one angle is (9x − 560)°
“the sum of … is (−18x + w)°”, “could NOT be the sum”
tm.ask: a constant in the sum, or the impossible sum
tm.rl: Write acute = a and obtuse = 180 − a; list every possible sum.
hd: Acute angles all equal a; obtuse angles all equal 180 − a.
Build each sum the question allows (e.g. 1 acute + 3 obtuse).
Match coefficients, or find the choice that is not on the list.
tr: Treating the sum as a single angle
Missing a combination of acute and obtuse angles

tm.nm: Parallel lines plus a triangle (or a bend)
tl: parallel lines with extra lines forming a triangle
a zigzag or bend between two parallel segments
a segment parallel to a leg (no figure)
tm.ask: an angle inside the figure
tm.rl: Move angles across the parallel lines first, then use the triangle sum (180) or a straight angle.
hd: Use the parallel lines to copy a known angle into the triangle.
Triangle sum 180; straight line 180.
For a bend: angle at the bend = sum of the two outside angles.
tr: Stopping at an intermediate angle
Using a supplementary angle where an equal one belongs

tm.nm: Which fact proves the lines parallel?
tl: several angles labeled at two intersections
“which additional information … lines are parallel”
tm.ask: the sufficient fact
tm.rl: Equal corresponding or alternate angles, or supplementary same-side interior angles, prove parallel.
hd: Find the pair of angles in the same position at the two intersections (or alternate positions).
They must be equal (or add to 180 for same-side interior).
tr: Choosing vertical angles at one intersection

tm.nm: Vertical angles, straight lines and exterior angles
tl: two or three lines crossing at a point
a triangle side extended (exterior angle)
a bowtie with angles in one triangle
tm.ask: an angle or the variable
tm.rl: Vertical angles are equal; a straight line is 180; exterior angle = sum of the two remote interior angles.
hd: Copy vertical angles across the crossing point.
Angles on a straight line add to 180.
Exterior angle = the two far interior angles added.
tr: Using the exterior angle as an interior angle

tm.nm: Angles in a triangle add to 180
tl: a triangle with two angles known (numbers or expressions)
a right triangle with one acute angle
Easy
tm.ask: the third angle or a variable
tm.rl: Sum = 180 (two acute angles of a right triangle sum to 90).
hd: Add the known angles; subtract from 180 (or 90).
If an angle is 2b, divide at the end.
tr: Forgetting to divide 2b by 2

tm.nm: Isosceles triangles: equal base angles
tl: “AB = BC”, two equal angles stated, or equal tick marks
one angle known directly or via a straight line
tm.ask: another angle, or which angle is impossible
tm.rl: Equal sides face equal angles; test both cases (given angle as apex, or as a base angle).
hd: Find the base angles (equal).
Apex = 180 − 2 × base.
If the given angle’s position is not stated, try it as the apex and as a base angle.
tr: Making the given angle the apex when it is a base angle

tm.nm: Chase angles through a multi-triangle figure
tl: two crossing segments inside a triangle
an isosceles condition (RT = TU)
two angles given far from the target
tm.ask: a far angle x
tm.rl: Label every angle you can, one fact at a time: straight lines, triangle sums, equal base angles.
hd: Start at the given angles; fill in straight-line partners.
Use the triangle sum to get each new angle.
Apply the isosceles condition to copy a base angle; finish with a triangle sum.
tr: Applying the isosceles condition to the wrong triangle

tm.nm: Similar or congruent figures: corresponding angles match
tl: “triangle ABC is congruent/similar to triangle DEF”, correspondence stated
a scale factor or side lengths (decoys for an angle question)
tm.ask: an angle
tm.rl: Matching letters have equal angles; scaling never changes angles.
hd: Match the asked angle to its partner by the order of the letters.
If needed, find the partner with the triangle sum.
tr: Using the scale factor on an angle (135 ÷ 5)
Matching letters in the wrong order

tm.nm: Similar triangles: sides by proportion (shadows, scale factors, areas)
tl: “similar”, a scale factor, or two objects and their shadows
one pair of corresponding sides known
sometimes an area
tm.ask: a side, a ratio, an area or a possible scale factor
tm.rl: Corresponding sides share one ratio; areas use the ratio squared.
hd: Pair corresponding sides by the letter order (or marked angles).
Scale factor = new ÷ old; multiply the matching side.
Areas: multiply by the scale factor squared.
tr: Pairing non-corresponding sides
Using the scale factor (not its square) for area
Inverting the factor

tm.nm: What proves similar, congruent or equilateral?
tl: two triangles with some parts given
“which additional information is sufficient to prove …”
I/II statements
tm.ask: the sufficient fact
tm.rl: Similar: AA or SAS with proportional sides. Congruent: SSS, SAS, ASA or AAS with equal sides.
hd: List what is already known (one angle pair, a side ratio).
Similar needs a second angle pair (find thirds by 180) or the including sides in the same ratio.
Congruent needs at least one pair of equal sides; angles alone give only similarity.
tr: Accepting AA for congruence
Using sides that do not include the known angle

tm.nm: A segment parallel to a side cuts proportionally
tl: a segment inside a triangle parallel to one side
three parallel lines across two transversals
lengths, a ratio or an area given
tm.ask: a length, the leftover piece, or which statements must be true
tm.rl: The small triangle is similar to the big one; parallel lines cut transversals in the same ratio.
hd: Small triangle ÷ big triangle gives the scale factor.
Find the small side, then subtract if the leftover piece is asked.
Three parallels: AB/BC = FE/ED.
tr: Answering the small triangle’s side instead of the leftover piece
Treating the cut piece as the whole side

tm.nm: Bowtie: two triangles meeting at a point
tl: two segments crossing at Q
parallel ends or two marked equal angles
lengths on both triangles
tm.ask: a length or an area
tm.rl: Vertical angles + one more angle pair = similar; match sides by the equal angles, not by position.
hd: Mark the vertical angles and the other equal pair.
Pair sides opposite equal angles; set one ratio.
tr: Pairing sides by where they sit on the page

tm.nm: Right isosceles triangles from coordinates
tl: vertices given as coordinates with legs parallel to the axes
tm.ask: an angle as an expression
tm.rl: Equal legs → 45° angles.
hd: Compute the leg lengths from the coordinates; equal legs give 45°.

tm.nm: Sine, cosine or tangent from a labeled triangle
tl: a right triangle with two sides labeled (or a 30° angle)
“what is the value of sin x°”
tm.ask: a trig ratio
tm.rl: SOH-CAH-TOA from the marked angle; a given angle alone fixes the ratio.
hd: From the marked angle: opposite, adjacent, hypotenuse.
sin = opp/hyp, cos = adj/hyp, tan = opp/adj; enter the fraction as is.
tr: Using the side adjacent to the angle for sine
Letting a decoy side length change the ratio

tm.nm: One trig ratio given: build the triangle and scale it
tl: “cos A = 3/5”, “tan X = 12/35”, “sin B = 5/13” with one side length
asks for another side, the perimeter, or a ratio of the other angle
tm.ask: a side, the perimeter or another ratio
tm.rl: Turn the ratio into a triple (3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 12-35-37), then scale to the given side.
hd: Write the ratio’s two sides on the triangle; get the third by Pythagoras (or a known triple).
Scale factor = given side ÷ its ratio side.
Multiply the side you need (or the whole perimeter) by the factor.
tr: The unscaled triple’s answer (84 instead of 168)
Matching the given side to the wrong part of the ratio
An unreduced ratio hiding the triple (24/51 = 8/17)

tm.nm: Complementary angles: sin A = cos(90° − A)
tl: “sin(R) = cos(S)”, angles x + 61 and 4x + 4
the two acute angles of one right triangle, or a right angle split in two
radians: angles add to π/2
tm.ask: x, a cofunction value, or an equivalent expression
tm.rl: If sin A = cos B for acute angles, A + B = 90° (π/2); tan of one = 1 ÷ tan of the other.
ds: Degree mode: type both expressions to compare numerically (e.g. (sin 24°)(cos 66°)+(cos 24°)(sin 66°))
hd: Set the two angles’ sum to 90 (or π/2) and solve.
sin of one acute angle = cos of the other; tan of one = reciprocal of the other.
Side lengths given alongside are usually decoys.
tr: Setting the two angles equal
Using π instead of π/2 for radians
Negative values for acute angles

tm.nm: Similar right triangles keep their trig ratios
tl: “triangle ABC is similar to triangle DEF, where A corresponds to D”
a trig value in one triangle; a scale factor that is a decoy
tm.ask: a trig ratio (or side) in the other triangle
tm.rl: Corresponding angles have equal ratios; the scale factor never matters for a ratio.
hd: Match the angle asked to its partner in the first triangle.
If it is the other acute angle, flip: tan → reciprocal, sin ↔ cos.
If only side lengths are listed, the right angle is opposite the longest side.
tr: Answering for the non-corresponding angle
Using the scale factor (2.9) in a ratio

tm.nm: Similar triangles inside a right triangle (parallel segment or altitude)
tl: a segment parallel to a leg, or an altitude to the hypotenuse
“figure above”, often no figure (sketch it)
tm.ask: a side or a trig ratio
tm.rl: The small triangle shares an angle with the big one; an altitude makes three similar triangles.
hd: Sketch and mark the shared angle (the altitude’s angle equals the far acute angle).
Set up one ratio of corresponding sides, or use the same tan on both triangles.
tr: Pairing the wrong sides
Using a decoy length (XY = 19)

tm.nm: Pythagorean theorem: a missing side
tl: two sides of a right triangle (or a rectangle’s diagonal and side)
“length of the hypotenuse/longer side”, “which equation/expression”
radicals like 4√82 or 10√37
tm.ask: the third side, or the equation or expression for it
tm.rl: a² + b² = c²; factor out a common multiple first.
ds: sqrt(9^2+6^2) (for “closest to” choices)
hd: Pull out a common factor: 10√37 and 24√37 → 10, 24 → 26√37.
Hypotenuse: √(a² + b²); leg: √(c² − a²).
tr: Adding the legs
Forgetting the square root
Doubling instead of squaring

tm.nm: Rectangle diagonal with sides x and x + k
tl: a rectangle’s diagonal √2,344
“one side is 8 more than the other”
tm.ask: the longer side
tm.rl: x² + (x + 8)² = diagonal²; answer the side asked.
ds: x^2+(x+8)^2=2344 | positive crossing x = 30; answer x + 8
hd: The asked side is x + 8 = 38.
tr: Answering x = 30

tm.nm: 30-60-90 and 45-45-90 triangles
tl: a 30°, 45° or 60° angle, “isosceles right”, or “diagonal twice the shortest side”
perimeters like 18 + 6√3 or 94 + 94√2
squares or rectangles in circles
tm.ask: a side, perimeter or diameter
tm.rl: Sides x : x√3 : 2x and x : x : x√2.
hd: Write the sides with one letter: 30-60-90 is x, x√3, 2x; 45-45-90 is x, x, x√2.
Match to the given length or perimeter and solve for x.
Answer the side asked (the longest, not x).
tr: Answering the short leg instead of the hypotenuse

ans.title: Numeric choices are listed in increasing order
ans.finding: When all four choices are numbers, College Board lists them smallest to largest in 603 of 722 questions (84%); 91 are largest to smallest.
ans.rule: Use the order to estimate: if your rough answer is about the middle size, look at B and C first.
ans.numbers: 603 of 722 numeric multiple-choice questions ascending, 91 descending, 28 unordered.

ans.title: D is right on 34% of Hard questions, but not because it is the largest number
ans.finding: On Hard multiple-choice questions D is the key in 132 of 387 (34%; 25% expected). Among Hard questions with numeric choices, the right answer is the largest value in only 46 of 181 (25%), and D is right in 51 of 181 (28%). The excess sits in non-numeric choices (expressions, equations, statements): D in 81 of 206 (39%).
ans.rule: Never pick a letter on purpose. As a last-resort guess on a Hard question with expression or statement choices, D is the least bad.

ans.title: The most common wrong choice is another quantity from the problem
ans.finding: Where College Board's explanation names what a wrong choice is, the largest group is a correctly computed value that answers a different question ("this is the value of x, not x − 5", "the pressure, not the temperature").
ans.rule: Before bubbling, reread the last sentence and check you are answering its quantity.
ans.numbers: At least 545 of 2,467 wrong-choice explanations (22%) match this pattern; sign errors 40, reciprocals 15, add-vs-multiply 49, percent/unit slips 60. The rest describe errors too specifically to classify by pattern.

ans.title: Grid-ins: fractions and decimals are common, negatives rare
ans.finding: Of 464 grid-in questions, 98 accept a fraction, 107 a decimal and 108 list several accepted forms; only 34 have a negative answer.
ans.rule: Grid fractions as fractions; if a decimal is long, enter as many digits as fit (College Board accepts .3833 and 0.383 for 23/60).
ans.numbers: 464 grid-ins: fraction 98, decimal 107, several forms 108, negative 34.

ans.title: Words that predict Hard
ans.finding: "Which of the following must be" (16.8× more common on Hard than Easy), "constant" (8.4×), "no solution / infinitely many / exactly one solution" (8.1×) and a positive/negative condition (4.8×) mark Hard questions. "Greatest/least possible" appears 6 times, all Hard. A table or figure is slightly less common on Hard (0.7×) and "equivalent" is less common (0.6×).
ans.rule: When you see these words, switch from computing to structure: compare coefficients, think about which root is allowed.
ans.numbers: must be: Easy 1/685, Hard 15/610; constant 19 vs 142; no/infinitely/exactly one 4 vs 29; positive/negative 13 vs 56; equivalent 54 vs 27.

ans.title: Templates that are always Hard
ans.finding: Some templates are Hard every time they appear: chained percent changes (12 of 12), a·bˣ + c (10 of 10), discriminant constants (17 of 17), no-solution constants (10 of 10), first-k-units pricing (7 of 7), parabola symmetry (7 of 7), squared units (6 of 6).
ans.rule: Learn these templates; they are the cheapest Hard points on the test.
ans.numbers: Counts from the per-skill template analysis (224 templates, 1,925 questions).

prob.intro: Probability on the SAT is mostly one move: a count divided by the right total. 46 questions are filed under Probability and conditional probability; another 20 in other skills (10 sample-to-population estimates, 8 nested percents, 2 margin-of-error counts) use the same idea.
prob.rule: The denominator is everyone who could be picked after you apply every condition in the question ("given that …", "of those …", "if the person chosen works in …", "one of the days on which …"). With no condition, it is the whole set.
prob.rule_check: 46 of 46 probability questions read individually (keyword matching alone gets 32 of 46, because "If … is selected at random from the box" names the whole set)

variants.name: One group, no condition: count ÷ total
tells: “selected at random” with no “given”, “of those” or “if … is”
counts in the text, a one-way table or a short list
choices in fraction, decimal or n/(n + k) form
variants.denominator: Denominator: everything that could be picked.
hand: Count the wanted outcome.
Divide by the total number of outcomes (add the table’s rows if there is no total).
Check place value: 4/1000 = 0.004.

variants.name: Count the qualifying outcomes first (neither, both, a range)
tells: “neither … nor …”, “even and at most 50”
counts or a range of integers to count from
variants.denominator: Denominator: the whole set. Do the counting before dividing.
hand: Turn the event into a count: neither blue nor yellow = red + white.
Divide by the whole set and reduce.
traps: Dividing by only the other categories (7/11) (1)

variants.name: Two-way table, no condition: row or column total ÷ grand total
tells: a two-way table with totals
“selected at random” and one feature, no “given”
hand: Find the row or column total for the feature.
Divide by the grand total.

variants.name: Two-way table, both features: one cell ÷ grand total
tells: two features joined by “and” or “has … and does not have …”
often no totals printed
variants.denominator: Denominator: the grand total (add all cells if no total is printed).
hand: Find the one cell with both features.
Add every cell for the denominator.
traps: A row or column total as the denominator (the conditional versions) (2)

variants.name: Two-way table, “given that” / “of those”: cell ÷ that row or column
tells: “given that”, “of the … that”, “if a … is selected from those who …”
a two-way table
variants.denominator: Denominator: the total of the group after “given that” / “of those”, never the grand total.
hand: Circle the group named after “given” or “of those”: its total is the denominator.
The numerator is the cell inside that group with the feature asked.
Give the form asked (fraction, decimal, percent).
traps: Condition reversed (the other margin as the denominator) (4)

variants.name: Conditional probability over combined rows or columns
tells: “at least”, “greater than”, “not in group 2” inside the condition
the condition covers two or more rows or columns
one-way table of ranges or percents
variants.denominator: Denominator: the sum of every row or column the condition covers (or 100% minus the excluded ones).
hand: List the rows or columns the condition covers; add their totals for the denominator.
Add the wanted cells inside them for the numerator.
With percents, use 100% minus the excluded rows as the denominator.
traps: Using only one of the covered columns (2)

variants.name: Conditional probability from counts described in words
tells: rows of trees, boxes of items: counts given as groups × per group
“given that”
variants.denominator: Build the hidden two-way table first.
hand: Multiply out each count (rows × per row).
Denominator: total of the given group; numerator: the wanted part of it.
traps: Using per-row counts and ignoring the different numbers of rows (1)

variants.name: Probability given, find a count
tells: “the probability … is 0.35” (or two probabilities)
“how many …”
variants.denominator: Count = probability × total; for the last category subtract the others from 1 first.
hand: If needed, P(last) = 1 − the others.
Multiply by the total.
traps: Answering the percent (28) instead of the count (98) (1)
Using the old total (83 million) instead of the stated one (1)

variants.name: Conditional probability given, solve for a missing cell
tells: a two-way table with x in one cell
“the probability … given … is 1/9”
variants.denominator: Write cell ÷ (group total with x) = given probability.
hand: Scale the fraction: 1/9 = 2/18, so the group total is 18 = 10 + x.

variants.name: Sample proportion × population (probability in disguise)
tells: "selected at random" sample, then "best estimate of the total number" in the population
choices are counts, often powers of ten apart
variants.denominator: The sample size: proportion = (count in sample) ÷ (sample size); then multiply by the population.
hand: Find the sample proportion.
Multiply by the population size (or classes × class size).
traps: Answering with the sample count itself (8 instead of 800)
Using the stated percent when the question asks for the complement (16,200 is choice A in 9ba3e283)
variants.checked: 555939d2: 8/300 × 30,000 = 800 (C); 9ba3e283: (1 − 0.346) × 26 × 1,800 = 30,607 ≈ 30,600 (C; the question asks for fewer than two siblings, a complement)

elsewhere.how: Sample percent × population = expected count; the sample size is the denominator.
"Of those, 37% …" is a conditional percent; the share of the whole is the product of the percents (a multiplication rule), and "not" is 1 minus it. 34f8cd89: 1 − 0.37×0.37×0.42 = 94.25%.
13f67ddc reads a probability of snow off a line graph (no computing).

notes: The site files 15 of the 18 one-group questions under "with a condition" (prb-given), though none has a condition: only 13 of its 42 prb-given questions are conditional.
Hard probability is almost all conditional: conditional-combined 4 of 5 Hard, table-conditional 3 of 7 Hard; the one-group template has 0 Hard of 18.
Desmos is rarely faster: these are one division. It helps only for summing several rows (conditional-combined) or to print a decimal to compare with decimal choices.

The turning point of a parabola is a clickable gray point.

Leave k undefined; Desmos offers a slider. Drag until the lines are parallel (no solution), coincide (infinitely many) or a line just touches a parabola.

Type y<6x+2 (and the other inequality); overlapping shading is the solution set; plot the choices as points.
Chained percents, volume formulas and conversions typed as one line.
Set Degrees in the wrench menu, or compare tan(92pi/3) with the choices in radians.

rules.evidence: Per-question "best" route over all 1,925 transcriptions. By template: 176 templates (1,321 questions) hand, 44 (546) either, 4 (58) Desmos.

rules.rule: Desmos pays off on Hard questions: 54 of the 92 Desmos-best questions are Hard and only 4 are Easy.
rules.evidence: Desmos-best by difficulty: Easy 4, Medium 34, Hard 54.

rules.rule: When the choices are expressions, solve by hand (or test one value of x); graph-matching expressions is rarely fastest.
rules.evidence: Expression choices: Desmos best in 5 of 465 questions, either in 19.

rules.rule: Use Desmos when the work is a system or a nonlinear equation you would otherwise have to rearrange: click intersections or zeros.

families.name: Coefficient matching for a constant
families.idea: Two sides that must be the same expression (or parallel/identical lines, or a double root) give one equation per matching coefficient; never solve for x.
spot: the word "constant" with "no solution", "infinitely many", "equivalent", "for all x" or "exactly one solution"
choices or answer are values of a letter, not of x
method: Write both sides in the same form.
No solution: same x-coefficients, different constants. Infinitely many: everything matches. Exactly one / no real solution for a quadratic: set the discriminant to 0 or < 0.
Solve the coefficient equation for the constant.
families.vs_patterns: Merges the site's "constant", "disguise" and "count" patterns: in the bank they are one move filed under four skills.

families.name: Scale factor k → k² → k³
families.idea: A length scale k multiplies areas by k² and volumes by k³; unit conversions of square and cubic units do the same.
spot: "similar", "scale", "each dimension is multiplied", square or cubic units being converted
method: Square it for area or square units, cube it for volume or cubic units.
families.vs_patterns: Not a site Big pattern; "ratio" (same shape, same ratio) covers lengths only. 32 of these questions are Hard.

families.name: Multiply the multipliers
families.idea: Percent changes, growth and chained "of those" percents are multiplication by factors; never add percents.
spot: two or more percent changes in a row
method: Turn each change into a factor (1 + p/100 or 1 − p/100, or p/100 for "of").
Multiply the factors; subtract 1 for the net change.
families.vs_patterns: Confirms the site's "multiplier" pattern and its "chained percents" rare pattern; the bank has 12 chained-change questions and all 12 are Hard.

families.name: a·bˣ + c: the starting value is a + c
families.idea: In an exponential with an added constant, the y-intercept and the long-run level both involve c; the coefficient alone is not the starting amount.
spot: f(x) = a·bˣ + c or a·bˣ − c
method: Plug in x = 0: f(0) = a + c.
The horizontal asymptote is y = c.
families.vs_patterns: New: exp-plus-constant has 10 questions, all Hard; the site's "form" pattern says the starting amount is printed in a·bˣ, which fails once a constant is added.

families.name: Symmetry of a parabola
families.idea: The vertex is halfway between the roots; sum of roots = −b/a; points with equal y-values sit symmetrically.
spot: two inputs with the same output
families.vs_patterns: Confirms the site's "symmetry" pattern; 42 of 50 questions are Hard.

families.name: First k units, then a rate
families.idea: A fixed charge or amount covers the first k units and a rate applies after that; the model uses (x − k).
spot: a flat fee that includes some units
method: Cost = fee + rate·(x − k) for x > k.
families.vs_patterns: New: lf/first-k-units has 7 questions, all Hard.

families.name: Distance, radius and Pythagoras
families.idea: Circle equations, right triangles, distances and diagonals are all a² + b² = c².
method: Complete the square if needed to read the radius; use a² + b² = c² for the missing length.

families.name: Similar triangles across skills
families.idea: Equal angles give equal side ratios; the same ratio drives side-splitter, altitude-to-hypotenuse and trig ratios.
spot: "similar", parallel segment inside a triangle, altitude to the hypotenuse, sin/cos given as a fraction
method: Match corresponding sides; set up one ratio.
families.vs_patterns: Confirms the site's "ratio" pattern; College Board splits it between two skills.

families.name: Divide by the right whole
families.idea: Probability, "percent of those" and sample-to-population estimates all need the right denominator.
spot: "given that", "of those", "selected at random", "best estimate of the total"
method: Denominator = everyone who could be picked after every condition; expected count = proportion × population.
families.vs_patterns: Confirms the site's "whole" pattern; see the probability atlas.

families.name: Two unknowns, two facts
families.idea: Stories with two kinds of items give a count total and a value total.
spot: two kinds of tickets/coins/items, "a total of"
method: x + y = count; ax + by = value; solve or click the intersection.

families.name: Plug in x = 1 (or a test value)
families.idea: For "sum of the coefficients" or equivalence, evaluating at one value replaces expanding.
method: Evaluate both sides at x = 1 (or 2); compare.
families.vs_patterns: New shortcut: sum of coefficients = p(1) (3 questions).

In the questions these are one move (match coefficients) across le1, sys, eqx and nle.
